Why I Build Software

What is most gratifying to me in this work is knowing that someone is using something I made with my intelligence and my hands; that it makes a task easier or allows the person to complete it more efficiently.

An employer or a client makes a project possible and deserves honest, competent work. But the purpose I hold onto while building is the person at the end of the chain: the person using the system in daily life, whose work, time or access to information is changed by what I deliver.

I write software to create bridges and shorten paths.

A Small Library System

Around twenty years ago, I built a small system for the library of an educational institution. I defined a code structure for books that allowed the library to arrange copies on shelves by affinity: category, work and copy. I also built an ASP 3 page on the local network so students in the laboratory could search not only for books, but inside their indexes, and see whether a copy was available or when it was expected back.

It was a small system. Its importance did not come from scale or technical fashion. It created a bridge between an institution, its books and its students. Each student who found material more easily received a concrete benefit from engineering work.

That remains a useful measure of professional satisfaction: the accumulated number of people who could do something more easily, reliably or safely because a system existed and was cared for.

Consequences For Engineering

This mission has practical consequences:

  • A feature is incomplete if it exists technically but is difficult for its intended user to find, understand or trust.
  • A small application deserves clear data handling, dependable behavior and usable documentation when people rely on it.
  • Performance, availability and accessible interaction matter because delay, outage and exclusion are experienced by people, not by architecture diagrams.
  • A technical shortcut is not harmless when it transfers recurring work, confusion or risk to users or maintainers.
  • Success is not measured only by delivery; it includes whether the software continues to serve its purpose responsibly.

Professional Boundary

Being oriented toward users does not mean ignoring legitimate business needs, budgets, deadlines or the judgment of colleagues. Software is produced inside real organizations with competing constraints. It means that, when discussing tradeoffs, the effect on the person who uses or depends on the system remains visible and is not treated as an afterthought.

The rest of this book translates that position into daily engineering practice.
